design.tex:
We implement the MDS-SMACOF algorithm using the \texttt{MDS} class in \texttt{sklearn.manifold}~\cite{scikit-learn}. Since we provide the shortest-path dissimilarity matrix $\{d^{\text{hop}}_{ij}\}$, we use \texttt{dissimilarity='precomputed'} unless stated otherwise. Two settings must be stated explicitly because their library defaults are inappropriate here. First, we set \texttt{n\_init=1}: the default \texttt{n\_init=4} performs four independent SMACOF runs per call and returns only the lowest-stress one, so an ensemble member would be the best of four draws rather than a single draw. Selecting the lowest-stress outcome from several starts changes the terminal sampling law relative to a single-start protocol; it does not, in general, imply a monotonic reduction in NEI. For the study, the SMACOF stopping tolerance is explicitly set to \texttt{eps=1e-12}; the earlier tolerance settings are for legacy calculations.  Table~\ref{tab:protocol_dependence} documents sensitivity under the legacy settings. Those comparisons do not establish the minimizer's uniqueness or replace numerical acceptance checks in the study. We use $p=2$ and 100 independent initialization attempts per graph, divided into two batches of 50. Initial coordinates are drawn independently from $U[0,1]$ in the original distance units. Each attempt uses a single SMACOF start, with
\texttt{n\_init=1}, \texttt{max\_iter=3000}, and
\texttt{eps=1e-12}. The SMACOF output is polished using L-BFGS-B. The primary settings are
\texttt{gtol=1e-14}, \texttt{ftol=1e-20},
\texttt{maxiter=50000}, \texttt{maxfun=200000}, and
\texttt{maxls=50}. Terminal configurations are evaluated against the declared numerical acceptance criteria before NEI is computed. The three empirical inputs in this study are unweighted. schoenberg.tex: Importantly, classical MDS provides the optimal positive-semidefinite rank-\(p\) approximation of the centered Gram matrix. Exact recovery with zero strain occurs only when the dissimilarities are Euclidean-realizable in at most \(p\) dimensions. SMACOF, by contrast, directly minimizes and optimizes the stress functional $F$ in Eq.~(\ref{eq:stress_function}), which is the operationally meaningful quantity for non-Euclidean dissimilarities.

fit.tex:
So far, we have worked at $p=2$ since its readability. The definition of NEI does not privilege that choice, so we ask how $\mathcal{I}$ depends on the embedding dimension. Two effects pull in opposite directions. Increasing $p$ enlarges the feasible configuration space, so the globally minimal stress cannot increase. At the same time, the extra degrees of freedom can open new directions along which distinct low-stress configurations become available, which would raise $\mathcal{I}$. The net effect is not obvious a priori.


Measuring $\mathcal{I}(p)$ for $p=1,\dots,20$ on the model networks (Fig.~\ref{fig:model_dim}) shows that the first effect dominates almost everywhere: $\mathcal{I}$ falls monotonically with $p$ for every model except the two regular lattices, and it does not saturate. At $p=20$ the
Erd\text{\H{o}}s--R\text{\'{e}}nyi graph reaches $\mathcal{I}=3\times10^{-7}$, the range occupied by the lattices at $p=2$. There is accordingly no characteristic dimension beyond which the measure
levels off, and we do not interpret $\mathcal{I}(p)$ as an estimator of an intrinsic embedding dimension. Two observations make that reading untenable. First, the shortest-path metric is not Euclidean-realizable at any small $p$: the hop distance on a square grid is the $\ell_1$ metric, which admits no isometric Euclidean embedding in any dimension, and the residual stress correspondingly plateaus at a nonzero value ($2607$ for the $10\times10$ grid) rather than vanishing. Second, the one model whose generative dimension is known---a random geometric graph drawn in the plane---shows no feature at $p=2$ whatsoever; its stress falls by more than half between $p=2$ and $p=3$ and $\mathcal{I}$ decreases monotonically throughout.

terminal.tex:
We first describe the distribution of numerically accepted terminal configurations without assuming that every terminal configuration is an exactly converged local minimum. A prescribed grouping partitions the accepted outcomes into terminal classes. Class membership describes geometric similarity at the chosen resolution and does not certify distinct minima. Exact stationarity together with a positive-definite Hessian on a regular slice transverse to the rigid-motion orbit is a sufficient local criterion for an isolated minimum modulo rigid motions; these are additional conditions, not consequences of grouping. Both $F_G$ and the pairwise distances $d_{ij}$ are $\mathrm{E}(p)$-invariant and therefore well defined on $\Omega$; this invariance is what makes the pairwise-distance ensemble the natural observable of the quotient landscape.

The SMACOF algorithm is a deterministic (by the given initial node positions) majorization-minimization procedure~\cite{borg2005modern}. The terminal ensemble is induced by the initialization law and the declared deterministic optimization procedure, rather than by thermal sampling. Numerical stationarity is assessed from the achieved full-gradient norm and the acceptance criteria, not inferred from monotone stress reduction or the requested stopping tolerance.

Initial coordinates are drawn uniformly from the bounded support $\Omega_0=[0,1]^{N\times p}$ used by the implementation. Let $\{\mathcal C_\gamma\}$ be a fixed measurable partition of the accepted pair-distance outcomes. For $\alpha_{G,\Pi}>0$, the class probabilities under the accepted law are
\begin{equation}
 P_\gamma
 =
 \Pr\!\left(D\in\mathcal C_\gamma
 \mid A_{\rm num},G,\Pi\right),
 \qquad
 \sum_\gamma P_\gamma=1.
 \label{eq:basin_occupancy}
\end{equation}
For uniform initialization on $\Omega_0$ and a deterministic terminal map, $P_\gamma$ equals the volume of accepted initial conditions leading to $\mathcal C_\gamma$, divided by the volume of all accepted initial conditions in $\Omega_0$. The normalization is therefore conditional on acceptance, rather than on the full initialization support alone. NEI is accordingly a property of the pair (topology, sampling protocol) — which is precisely the operational claim we make, and the reason all networks and null models are sampled under an identical protocol.

hessian.tex: Two properties govern how $H$ may be read. First, the $p$ translations are exact null directions at any configuration, because the stress depends only on coordinate differences. At a stationary configuration, differentiating rotational invariance implies that each rotational tangent lies in the kernel of $H$. Away from stationarity, the identity $v^{\mathsf T}Hv=-\nabla F_G\!\cdot\!X''(0)$ does not generally imply a rotational null mode. We project $H$ onto the orthogonal complement of the rigid-motion tangent space constructed at each terminal configuration. Stationarity is assessed separately using the full coordinate-gradient norm, together with optimizer termination information and iteration counts.

rigidity.tex:
Second, in the zero-residual limit $\delta_{ij}=d_{ij}$ the second term of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:hess_block} vanishes and $H=2R^{\mathsf{T}}WR$ with $R$ a rigidity
matrix. The framework in question is the \emph{complete} one: the stress imposes
a dissimilarity on every node pair, not on the edges of $G$. Sparsity of $G$
therefore does not make the framework underconstrained, since a complete
framework is generically rigid for $N>p+1$. At finite residual, a prestress
contribution is added to $H$, and small or negative eigenvalues may originate
from that term or from geometric degeneracy rather than from a continuous
deformation mode~\cite{connelly1996second}

Accordingly, we report a small
$\lambda_{\min}$ as a near-zero projected curvature mode and make no claim of a
continuous floppy manifold; establishing one requires continuation along the
corresponding eigenvector to exhibit an actual low-stress path.

gate.tex:
If $M_{\rm adm}<2$, or if any empirical pair mean is zero, we withhold the NEI estimate.
We neither remove pairs after observing the outcomes nor introduce a regularization constant into the denominator. The algebraic zero obtained from a single accepted run is not reported as evidence of reproducibility.

We report $\mathcal I$ together with
$\widehat{\alpha}_{G,\Pi}$, $M_{\rm adm}$, and sampling uncertainty. Uncertainty is assessed using complete accepted run vectors because distances within the same embedding are dependent.
A small sample NEI indicates a narrow sampled distance ensemble; it does not establish the uniqueness of the embedding or determine the number of minima.

NEI.tex:
Provided that $\bar d_{ij}>0$ for every pair in $\mathcal P$, the relative pairwise variability is
\begin{equation}
r_{ij}
=\frac{\sigma_{ij}^{2}}{\bar d_{ij}^{\,2}},
\qquad (i,j)\in\mathcal P.
\label{eq:rel_pair}
\end{equation}
The sample network embedding inconsistency is
\begin{equation}
\mathcal I
=\frac{1}{Q}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal P}r_{ij}.
\label{eq:NEI}
\end{equation}
Here, $\mathcal I$ denotes the finite-sample estimate of relative
pair-distance variability under the accepted law
$\mu^{\rm adm}_{G,\Pi}$.

If $M_{\rm adm}<2$, or if any empirical pair mean is zero, we withhold the NEI estimate.
We neither remove pairs after observing the outcomes nor introduce a regularization constant into the denominator. The algebraic zero obtained from a single accepted run is not reported as evidence of reproducibility.

We report $\mathcal I$ together with
$\widehat{\alpha}_{G,\Pi}$, $M_{\rm adm}$, and sampling uncertainty. Uncertainty is assessed using complete accepted run vectors because distances within the same embedding are dependent.
A small sample NEI indicates a narrow sampled distance ensemble; it does not establish the uniqueness of the embedding or determine the number of minima.

Both $r_{ij}$ and $\mathcal I$ are dimensionless.
For a fixed accepted ensemble, a common rescaling
$d_{ij}^{(m)}\mapsto a\,d_{ij}^{(m)}$ with $a>0$ leaves $\mathcal I$ unchanged: the variance and squared mean both scale by $a^2$.
This algebraic invariance does not, by itself, establish invariance under rescaling of the input metric; this also depends on how the initialization, optimization, and acceptance rules transform under that rescaling.

The grouping resolution as a declared analysis parameter and evaluates $\varepsilon_D\in\{10^{-6},10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\}$. Perturb-and-reoptimize calibration is not part of the present grouping procedure.
We do not report a grouping at a single threshold. At each resolution, complete-link clustering of the accepted discovery-batch outcomes defines frozen terminal classes. A validation outcome is assigned only if it lies within $\varepsilon_D$ of every member of exactly one discovery class; otherwise, it is recorded as unmatched or ambiguous. Recurrence is reported as a separate diagnostic and is not used to exclude accepted runs from NEI.

multiplicity.tex: We treat embedding variability as a diagnostic observable of a specified graph-to-embedding procedure. Random initialization is the sampling device; even when it is the only stochastic input (the initial position), the dispersion of terminal outputs can depend on the graph through the deterministic stress-minimization map. Accordingly, we test for differences between observed graphs and matched null ensembles under a common protocol, rather than posing algorithmic and structural variation as mutually exclusive alternatives. We use initialization-sensitive terminal variability to describe geometric differences among numerically accepted outcomes under the specified protocol. Interpreting this variability as embedding multistability requires additional evidence that recurrent, geometrically separated terminal classes correspond to distinct local minima. NEI alone neither counts minima nor establishes uniqueness when its value is small. Structural multistability is therefore the phenomenon this work targets, and NEI is the protocol-conditioned observable that bounds it rather than a count of it: the accepted terminal ensemble is what we measure, and the additional evidence required to convert a wide ensemble into a statement about distinct minima is stated explicitly wherever it is not available.

We first examine whether fixing the degree sequence is sufficient
to account for the observed terminal spread. For each anchor graph, we compare its accepted NEI with the mean over the declared
degree-preserving null ensemble. The examined degree-four ring and square lattice have lower accepted NEI than their rewired controls. We next apply the same comparison to three empirical inputs to examine the scope of this pattern.

The  empirical analysis comprises three unweighted inputs. For ca-sandi-auths, 21 of 100 attempts passed the numerical gate, and the primary degree-preserving contrast was $-0.01778$, with a nested resampling sensitivity interval $[-0.03683,-0.00315]$.  For ENZYMES-g295, 42 attempts were accepted. Its primary contrast was $0.00014$, with interval $[-0.00807,0.00815]$, leaving the direction unresolved. For eco-foodweb-baywet, nine attempts were accepted, and the null-ensemble contrasts were withheld because some requested null graphs lacked an estimable NEI.  These examples provide case-specific comparisons of accepted terminal spread under the declared protocol. They do not establish a common ordering across empirical network categories. The two layers of evidence must be kept apart. The $84$-network survey of Tables~\ref{tab:real_network_summary_IS} and~\ref{tab:real_network_summary_IS_added} is run under one fixed protocol for every graph and its two nulls, but without the numerical acceptance gate, so its entries are terminal spreads of all completed attempts rather than of gate-passing attempts; the three inputs above are the only ones evaluated under the gate, and there the acceptance rate ranges from $9\%$ to $42\%$. We therefore read the survey as a protocol-matched comparison across graphs and the gated examples as the statement of what survives the stationarity requirement, and we do not quote a survey value as a gate-passing one.

The corrected empirical comparisons are case specific: ca-sandi-auths exhibits a negative primary degree-preserving contrast, ENZYMES-g295 remains directionally unresolved under the primary settings, and the eco-foodweb-baywet contrasts are withheld because the requested null ensembles are not fully estimable. These results do not establish a common reduction across empirical networks or identify a particular higher-order structural mechanism.

The connected $G(N,E)$ reference ensemble fixes the node and edge counts but does not preserve the empirical degree sequence or higher-order organization. Individual null realizations may nevertheless exhibit degree heterogeneity, correlations, and apparent modular structure. It therefore serves as a baseline for embedding variability under randomized connectivity with matched size. In contrast, the degree-preserving null model, generated by repeated double-edge swaps~\cite{Maslov2002Specificity}, preserves the degree sequence and thus controls for one of the most basic forms of structural heterogeneity. Comparisons with these ensembles assess terminal variability relative to different structural constraints; they do not constitute an additive or causal decomposition of size, density, degree sequence, and higher-order organization.

recur.tex:
The grouping resolution as a declared analysis parameter and evaluates $\varepsilon_D\in\{10^{-6},10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\}$. Perturb-and-reoptimize calibration is not part of the present grouping procedure.
We do not report a grouping at a single threshold. At each resolution, complete-link clustering of the accepted discovery-batch outcomes defines frozen terminal classes. A validation outcome is assigned only if it lies within $\varepsilon_D$ of every member of exactly one discovery class; otherwise, it is recorded as unmatched or ambiguous. Recurrence is reported as a separate diagnostic and is not used to exclude accepted runs from NEI.

resid.tex:
Second, in the zero-residual limit $\delta_{ij}=d_{ij}$ the second term of
Eq.~\eqref{eq:hess_block} vanishes and $H=2R^{\mathsf{T}}WR$ with $R$ a rigidity
matrix. The framework in question is the \emph{complete} one: the stress imposes
a dissimilarity on every node pair, not on the edges of $G$. Sparsity of $G$
therefore does not make the framework underconstrained, since a complete
framework is generically rigid for $N>p+1$. At finite residual, a prestress
contribution is added to $H$, and small or negative eigenvalues may originate
from that term or from geometric degeneracy rather than from a continuous
deformation mode~\cite{connelly1996second}

Egap.tex: The stress objective defines an optimization landscape, whereas NEI summarizes the relative spread of pair distances among the accepted terminal ensemble sampled on that landscape. In this view, the MDS embedding process corresponds to minimizing the stress function in Eq.~\eqref{eq:stress_function} over a continuous configuration space. Different initializations can produce geometrically distinct terminal configurations. Interpreting their spread as multiplicity of local minima requires additional validation; equal-energy degeneracy further requires evidence of energy equivalence.
